answer.evidence: The light grey top band (L about 145-148) covers rows 8-13 at x=4 and rows 11-13 at x=8. The silhouette widens from 5 to 16 px over rows 7-15, which fits a broken, sloping top. Row 14 is a lighter front-edge line (L=189, #bcbdc3). Below it the face is darker (L about 112), so rows 15-16 read as eave shadow. The front face runs from row 15 to row 31, about 17 rows, with a lighter course line at row 22. The reddish-brown pixels at x=11, rows 10-13, are the rebar and count as decor. They are not the main body.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny prop beside two full houses, so it is judged mainly on the measured facts. It carries 10 visible tones per 16x16 tile, against 12 for h101 and 10 for the stone house h112, so it is level with the closest reference. Near-flat coverage is only 8%, so there are no large flat fills; the top slab, front face and broken edge each show grain and tone changes. Only 2% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outline leans toward the material (dark tinted grey-brown beside the concrete and a reddish tone at the rebar) and does not read as a black sticker line. The concrete ramp has about 4 steps (top highlight, light, mid, dark crack/shadow), a little fewer than the roughly 6 steps in the references. The total palette is small (13 colours), but the visible texture is about as rich as the stone wall reference at this scale. A careful artist would accept it next to the references, so it passes, though it is slightly less rich than they are.
